【Tianfeng Securities Overseas Technology】
Takeaways from an Interview with SanDisk IRD

1. Pricing remains a slightly larger contributor to FY27 Q1 earnings growth, but it is reasonable to estimate that pricing and volume each account for roughly half.

2. Volumes under long-term agreements are also fixed, with no room for adjustment. In many cases, volumes are specified not only annually but also quarterly or even monthly. Product types—including TLC/QLC and process nodes—are also explicitly stipulated.

3. HBF is not taking away HBM’s addressable market; it represents an additional memory tier. It is specifically designed for inference rather than training. In inference workloads, read operations significantly outnumber write operations.

4. YMTC is expected to capture an 80% share of the Chinese market. However, China’s market is growing so rapidly that even this would not be enough to satisfy demand. The impact of YMTC’s capacity expansion is material, but it is unlikely to become a major risk to global supply and demand over the next several years.

5. Asian investors are concerned about price declines in Q4 and Q1. However, the company has seen no signs of pricing deterioration to date and does not expect a material change in the 2027 supply-demand balance. The market remains tight. In fact, NBM customers are returning to request higher volumes or longer contract durations.

6. Finally, the company was asked, “What is the market’s biggest misconception about SanDisk?” The response remained extremely bullish. The market is still adjusting to a “new reality”—the sustainability of the business has fundamentally changed. Despite the company providing a range of supporting metrics, the market continues to question the sustainability of its business model.“The market is essentially telling you that the company’s terminal value is zero.”

$NVDA $NBIS $CRWV $IREN 

Nvidia just told its biggest customers that servers with its AI chips are going up more than 15%, with memory costs the main driver. It hits the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems, and Microsoft, Google and Oracle have already been notified.

Here’s what that means for NeoClouds.

The squeeze hits anyone who owns their GPUs on fixed-price contracts that aren’t built yet. Revenue locked, hardware bill up. What separates the winners is contract structure: how short you run, how fast you reprice, and who funds the build.

$NBIS is best positioned. It deliberately runs midterm and short-term deals and left 2027 capacity unsold so it can reprice, and it proved that power with a capacity auction that cleared 15% above any rate it had ever charged and 20% above current Blackwell pricing. New deals are at $20m+/MW, short-term above $40m, and ~70% of Q2 bookings came prepaid covering half the capex. Pricing-power side, not locked-in-cheap.

$IREN is interesting because its Microsoft deal has the GPUs ~95% pre-funded through Dell financing and Microsoft’s prepayment, so the hardware cost isn’t really IREN’s to eat, and it’s still signing new deals at ~2-year paybacks.

$CRWV is the split case. It’s repricing new contracts up ~25% with higher margins, so the front book has pricing power too. But it owns its GPUs, carries $35B+ in debt, and its big long-dated legacy book (Microsoft especially) is exactly where the squeeze lands. Better than the fixed-lease miners, more exposed than NBIS because it runs longer contracts and funds the build with debt, not prepayments.

Nobody who owns GPUs is fully immune: already-signed, unbuilt deals get squeezed for all of them. The difference is how much of the book is locked cheap versus repriceable.

As for the root cause: memory.

It has stopped being a swing component and started acting structural. Its pricing is becoming less cyclical and more permanent. The scarcity that’s already lifted the memory names is now taxing every AI server shipped. 

TL;DR This is brutal for fixed-price contracts that are largely unbuilt, better for anyone repricing forward, and the colos that just rent out space while clients bring their own compute stay largely insulated.

$INDI up +6% on the day, and the more I dig into it the more I like it. What @CKCapitalxx  found digging through the filings is the kind of thing you can't unsee once you've seen it.

Indie is five companies reported as one.

On the surface it's an automotive chip maker. Image signal processors and radar, the silicon that turns a camera's raw sensor data into something a car can act on in under thirty milliseconds. 

But per CK's deep dive, underneath that one segment sit four more that never get named on an earnings call:

Industrial radar, out of Germany. Not automotive. 

This is radar that stops cranes crushing people, tracks containers at ports, runs telemetry on locomotives. And the detail that makes it huge for me.

It's certified to the European machine-safety standard. 

That is the exact certification a machine needs to operate next to a human. Which is to say, the exact certification a humanoid robot needs. It's a robotics moat if you look at it from another angle.

Photonics, out of Switzerland. Light sources for fiber-optic gyroscopes, which is how aircraft and defense systems navigate when GPS is jammed.

A quantum laser. A specific wavelength whose only real buyer is someone building a quantum computer.

Plus the Chinese subsidiary everyone treats as a drag on the accounts.

Four brand names, several countries, one company.

Nobody models them separately because indie doesn't break them out. 

CK did the work of pulling them apart, and the picture that emerges is a company being valued as a single-product automotive supplier while quietly holding a portfolio of businesses in radar, photonics, defense-adjacent navigation, and quantum.

The robot thesis, that automotive perception transfers to humanoids, is real and I believe it. But it treats indie as a one-trick chip company that got lucky with robotics inbound. 

Per CK this is already a multi-domain sensing company, and the market is paying for one domain.

At roughly a $920m market cap, you're buying the automotive business and getting radar, photonics, and a quantum laser thrown in for free, along with the robotics optionality.

The risk is still really big when playing a name like this, so size it as the binary risk/reward that it is.
